    Gluten-Free Memorial Day Recipes for an Easy Cookout

    May 13, 2026 By J. B. Maer Leave a Comment

    By
    J. B. Maer     / Last Modified On May 13, 2026
    Listen to audio version of this article
    Sponsored by
    0:00 / 8:32
    Instaread

    The first Memorial Day after my celiac diagnosis, I stood in my mother-in-law's kitchen holding a paper plate and a hot dog bun I knew I couldn't eat, and I cried in the pantry for about four minutes. Then I came back out and ate a hamburger patty with a fork. I told everyone I was on a new diet.

    That was a long time ago. The menu I make now is the menu my whole family eats, and most of them don't have celiac. Nobody cries in the pantry anymore. The cookout is the cookout.

    This is the gluten-free Memorial Day menu I actually use. Mains off the grill, sides that survive a forty-minute drive to a friend's house, and dessert. Twelve recipes. One menu. No more standing in front of the cooler making a calculation about which condiment to use.

    Off the grill: the mains

    The grill is where Memorial Day either works or falls apart. The food has to be good enough that no one notices it's gluten-free, and easy enough that you're not stuck flipping burgers while everyone else is in the pool.

    I start with easy gluten-free meatballs. They're a make-ahead and they reheat well in a slow cooker. They're also the first thing to disappear from the table every single year. The recipe uses gluten-free breadcrumbs and an egg as binder, and they hold their shape on a toothpick. Set them out with a small jar of toothpicks and walk away. Done.

    Burgers are the obvious main, and the bun is the hard part. I use the homemade gluten-free hot dog buns for hot dogs and the gluten-free hamburger buns for everything else. The hamburger buns hold up to a juicy patty without falling apart, which is the actual test. Most store-bought GF buns turn to wet cardboard around minute three of a burger. These don't.

    If you want a main that isn't a burger, gluten-free chicken wings are it. I toss them in homemade gluten-free BBQ sauce because most store-bought BBQ sauces have a soy sauce or malt issue I don't want to think about on a Saturday. The wings go on the grill at the start of the cookout and they're gone by the time the burgers are off.

    And for kids, or anyone who wants something between a hot dog and a burger, the gluten-free sloppy joes are perfect. Make them in the morning and hold them warm in a slow cooker.

    Scoop onto a GF bun when someone asks. The mess is the point. Best eaten outdoors!

    Memorial Day sides that travel well

    Sides are where most Memorial Day spreads either shine or get sad. I keep a few rules. No mayonnaise sides in direct sun. Anything with potatoes gets made the night before. Coleslaw is mandatory.

    The gluten-free coleslaw is the one I make every year. It uses a simple dressing that doesn't break when it sits, and the cabbage stays crunchy for hours. It fills out a paper plate without competing with anything else on it.

    For potato salad, I make the vegan potato salad because it travels safer than a mayo version and almost no one can tell. It's bright and tangy, and it keeps in a cooler for the whole afternoon without me checking on it.

    If you're contributing to someone else's cookout instead of hosting, easy spinach dip is the move. Bring it in a bowl with a bag of gluten-free crackers or veggies and you've handled your end of the spread with one trip to the kitchen.

    The last side is gluten-free pasta salad, which is the one dish my non-GF brother-in-law specifically asks me to bring. Use a sturdy gluten-free pasta (corn-and-rice blends hold up better than chickpea on a hot day) and dress it the night before. Let it sit. Better the second hour than the first.

    Side salads are also easy. If you're prepping them ahead of time, just wait to add dressing. I'm a fan of Mediterranean style salads with fresh flavors like salty feta and olives. You can also add fresh mint, zucchini, beans, or even cheddar cheese.

    Snacks and starters

    The hour before the food is ready is the hour people get cranky. A few well-placed snacks fix that.

    Gluten-free sausage balls are an old-school appetizer that works on a paper plate, with one hand, in a folding chair. They're cheesy and savory, and they pair with a beer or a lemonade equally well. Make a double batch.

    Crack corn dip is the one I make when I want the table to gather around something. It's sweet and a little spicy, and you can eat it with a GF chip or a spoon (no judgment). I've watched a bowl of this disappear inside ten minutes at a family party.

    For something a little more involved, jalapeño poppers are worth the extra step. They prep in the morning and bake while the grill is heating up. Plate them with toothpicks and they vanish.

    Memorial Day Desserts

    Dessert is the easiest part. Strawberries and chocolate carry the holiday, and the gluten-free versions are as good as anything you'd buy.

    The easy gluten-free chocolate cake is the recipe I have memorized. Eleven ingredients, one bowl, an hour from start to plate. It is fudgy and rich and the kind of dessert that gets eaten in two slices, cold, the morning after the cookout. I won't pretend this is sophisticated. It's the cake.

    Gluten-free strawberry shortcake is the seasonal pick. Memorial Day weekend is peak strawberry season in a lot of the country, and a buttery biscuit with macerated berries and real whipped cream is hard to beat. I assemble these on the fly so the biscuit doesn't get soggy.

    For the kids, or for the adult who doesn't want a slice of cake, a pitcher of strawberry watermelon smoothie covers it. It looks like summer in a glass and it uses up the watermelon you bought, which you will not finish otherwise.

    More gluten-free summer recipes

    If you want to round out the table, the gluten-free bread recipe works for slider buns in a pinch. The gluten-free BBQ sauce is worth trying on its own. We use that year-round, but it's especially helpful during barbecue season.

    We also love steak, burgers, and brats. When it comes to Memorial Day recipes, crowd favorites are always on the grill.  Just make sure to stock up on lettuce, condiments, onions, and tomatoes for toppings. And if you're really looking to impress this year, try sautéing mushrooms and garlic in butter and serving it as an optional topping for any grilled meats.

    Frequently Asked Questions

    Are hot dogs and hamburger buns the hardest part of a gluten-free cookout?

    For most people, yes. Store-bought gluten-free buns vary widely in quality, and a bad bun can tank an otherwise great burger. Making your own buns the morning of the cookout solves it, or buying a fresh brand from the bakery section (not frozen) gets close. My hamburger buns recipe is the one I rely on every year.

    What can I bring to a Memorial Day potluck if I'm gluten-free?

    Bring a dish you can eat. The spinach dip with gluten-free crackers, the pasta salad, the vegan potato salad, and the chocolate cake are all great potluck contributions. You guarantee yourself one safe option and the host doesn't have to think about it.

    Can I cook gluten-free food on a shared grill?

    You can, with caution. Clean the grates with a wire brush before adding gluten-free food, or lay down a sheet of foil for your GF items. If you have celiac and the grill regularly cooks marinated meats with soy sauce or beer in the marinade, the risk is higher than if it's mostly used for plain proteins.

    What's a good gluten-free dessert that travels?

    The chocolate cake travels well in a covered cake plate or a 9x13 pan. Sausage balls and dips travel in any container with a tight lid. Strawberry shortcake is the one to assemble on-site, since the biscuit gets soft if you stack it with the berries too early.

    Are most BBQ sauces gluten-free?

    Many are, but not all. Watch for soy sauce, malt vinegar, or so-called "natural flavors" without clarification on the label. Brands that explicitly label gluten-free are the safer bet. I make my own when I want to be sure, and the recipe is in the BBQ chicken section above.
